analogy.p: Think of the computer as a restaurant. The customers are the users and the chefs are the applications. The manager (the OS) seats customers (user interface), shares out kitchen space so chefs do not get in each other's way (memory management), makes sure each chef gets a turn at the oven (multitasking), uses the right suppliers' ordering systems for each delivery (drivers), checks who is staff and who is a guest (user management) and files all the orders so they can be found later (file management). The analogy breaks down because a real manager does not have to switch between hundreds of tasks every few milliseconds, and the OS also controls the physical equipment directly.
analogy.t: The OS is the manager of a busy restaurant

bullets: The OS is **system software**: software that runs and maintains the computer itself, as opposed to **application software** that does a task for the user (a word processor, a game).
Its **purpose** is to manage the hardware and software resources of the computer and to provide an interface so that users and applications can use them.
Examples you should recognise: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS. A laptop, a phone and a games console each run an OS.
The OS is loaded into RAM from secondary storage during the **boot** process, after the BIOS/firmware has started the computer; it stays in RAM while the computer is on.
The five functions in the specification are not separate programs: they are jobs the OS does at the same time, all the time.
Why it matters: applications ask the OS for resources (memory, file access, printing) rather than controlling the hardware themselves, which stops programs interfering with each other.
Link to other topics: the CPU runs the OS instructions using the fetch-decode-execute cycle (1.1.1), and the OS lives in RAM (1.2.1).
core.h: What an operating system is and why every computer needs one
core.p: An **operating system (OS)** is **system software** that manages the computer's hardware and provides a platform on which application software can run. Without one, every program would have to contain its own code to talk to the keyboard, screen, memory and storage, which would be slow to write, wasteful and unsafe. OCR J277 1.5.1 asks you to explain the purpose of an OS and to describe its main functions: the **user interface**, **memory management and multitasking**, **peripheral management and drivers**, **user management** and **file management**. Think of the OS as the manager that sits between the user, the applications and the hardware.

bullets: **User interface**: lets the user interact with the computer, for example by clicking icons or typing commands.
**Memory management**: allocates RAM to programs and the OS, keeps each program's memory separate and frees it when finished.
**Multitasking**: runs several programs at once by giving each a short slice of CPU time in turn.
**Peripheral management**: controls input, output and storage devices, using **device drivers** to translate between the OS and each device.
**User management**: creates and controls user accounts, passwords and access rights.
**File management**: creates, names, organises, moves, copies, deletes and secures files in a folder (directory) structure.
In the exam the usual command words are *State* (name a function), *Describe* (say what it does) and *Explain* (say what it does and why it matters).
Common 6-mark pattern: *Discuss the functions of an operating system*. Cover at least four functions, each with a description and a consequence for the user.
core.h: The five functions at a glance
core.p: The specification lists a small set of functions and expects you to be able to name them and give a short, accurate description of each. A good way to learn them is as five questions the OS answers. How does the user talk to the computer (user interface)? Where does each running program live and how do they share the CPU (memory management and multitasking)? How do the keyboard, screen and printer work (peripheral management and drivers)? Who is allowed to use the computer and what can they do (user management)? Where and how is data stored and found (file management)?

bullets: **GUI**: uses **windows, icons, menus and a pointer**. Advantages: easy for beginners, no commands to remember, visual feedback. Disadvantages: uses more memory and processing power, and can be slower for experienced users to perform repetitive tasks.

**CLI**: the user types commands at a prompt. Advantages: uses little memory, very fast for experts, can run scripts that automate many tasks. Disadvantages: the user must learn exact commands and syntax; a typing mistake causes an error.
Other styles you may meet: **touchscreen** interfaces (taps and swipes on phones) and **voice** interfaces, both of which are still managed by the OS.
The UI is the **only** part of the OS most users ever see, so it strongly affects how easy a computer is to use.
A good interface should be **intuitive**, consistent, give clear feedback and be accessible (for example large text or screen readers for users with disabilities).
The OS draws the windows, tracks the mouse, and sends key presses to the program that has **focus** (the active window).
Why not just use a CLI everywhere? Most users are non-technical, so GUIs make computers usable by everyone; but servers often use a CLI because it needs fewer resources.
core.h: User interface: how people control the computer
core.p: The **user interface (UI)** is the part of the OS that the user sees and uses to give instructions and receive information. Two types matter for GCSE: the **graphical user interface (GUI)** and the **command-line interface (CLI)**. A GUI uses windows, icons, menus and pointers (often called **WIMP**), which makes it easy to learn because you point and click. A CLI needs the user to type exact text commands, which is harder to learn but very powerful and fast for experts. The OS must also pass your input to the correct application and show that application's output on screen.

bullets: **Allocation**: when a program is opened the OS finds free RAM for it, loads its instructions and data, and records the address range it has been given.

**Protection**: each program is kept in its own area of memory. If one crashes, the OS can close it without the others being corrupted; this is why one frozen app does not normally bring down the whole computer.
**Freeing memory**: when a program closes, its RAM is marked free for other programs to use. If memory is not freed properly the system gradually slows down.

**Virtual memory**: when RAM is nearly full the OS moves data that is not currently needed from RAM to a reserved area of the hard drive, and brings it back when needed. This lets more programs run than RAM alone could hold.
Why virtual memory is slower: secondary storage is much slower than RAM, so heavy use causes the computer to slow down (sometimes called **thrashing**). The fix is to add more RAM.
The OS itself needs a share of RAM, which is why a computer with 8 GB of RAM never has the full 8 GB free for your programs.
Link to topic 1.2.1: RAM is **volatile**, so everything in memory is lost when power is off and must be saved to secondary storage first.
core.p: **Memory management** is the OS function that controls how **RAM** is used. Programs and data must be loaded into RAM before the CPU can use them, but RAM is limited and many programs want it at the same time. The OS decides where each program is loaded, keeps a record of which parts of RAM are in use, and makes sure one program cannot read or overwrite the memory belonging to another program or to the OS. When a program closes, the OS frees its memory so that it can be reused.

bullets: The CPU switches between programs so quickly that it looks as if they run **at the same time**; this is called **multitasking**.

Each program is allowed to run for a short **time slice**; when it ends, the OS saves where the program had reached and loads the next one. This keeps the CPU busy and gives every program a fair share.
A **multi-core** CPU can genuinely run more than one program at once (one on each core), but the OS still multitasks when there are more programs than cores.
Multitasking depends on memory management: all the programs that are taking turns must have their instructions and data in RAM (or virtual memory) at once.
The OS also decides **priority**: for example the program you are using (the foreground window) usually gets more CPU time than a background update.
Why it matters: the user does not have to wait for one task to finish before starting another, and the CPU is not left idle while a program waits for slow input or output.
Common error: saying that the CPU runs all programs at exactly the same time. On a single core it runs one at a time, very quickly in turn.
core.p: **Multitasking** means the computer appears to run several programs at the same time, for example playing music while you write an essay and download a file. A CPU core can only execute one instruction stream at a time, so the OS shares the processor between programs using **time slices**. Each running program is given a very short turn (a few milliseconds) and then the OS switches to the next one. Because the switching is so fast the user sees what looks like simultaneous running. The part of the OS that decides whose turn it is, is called the **scheduler**.

bullets: A **device driver** is software that allows the OS to communicate with a hardware device by translating between them.
Every device needs a driver; many are built into the OS so a new mouse works instantly (**plug and play**), while others must be installed from the manufacturer.
Drivers allow **many different brands** of printer or graphics card to work with the same OS, because the OS only has to talk to the driver, not the hardware.
Without the correct, up-to-date driver a device may not work, or may work badly. **Updating drivers** can fix bugs and improve performance.
The OS handles **input and output**: it receives key presses and mouse clicks and passes them to the correct program, and sends output to the screen, speakers or printer.
For printing, the OS uses a **print queue** (buffer): jobs are stored and sent to the printer in order, so the user can carry on working while the printer is slow.
Interrupts: a device signals the CPU when it needs attention (for example a key press), and the OS handles it, so the CPU does not waste time constantly checking.
Link to other topics: peripherals include secondary storage devices (1.2.2) and input/output devices (1.1.3 embedded systems use similar principles).
core.p: A **peripheral** is any hardware device connected to the computer that is not the CPU or main memory, such as a keyboard, mouse, monitor, printer, scanner or external drive. **Peripheral management** is the OS function that controls communication between the computer and these devices. Every device speaks its own language, so the OS uses a small program called a **device driver** for each one. The driver translates general instructions from the OS (for example 'print this page') into the exact commands that the particular device understands, and translates the device's replies back.

bullets: Each user has a **username and password** (or biometric such as fingerprint) so the OS can **authenticate** them before access.
**Access rights** (permissions) decide which files, folders, programs and settings each user can open, change or delete.
**Administrator accounts** have full control; **standard** or **guest** accounts are restricted. Restricting rights limits the damage if an account is misused or infected with malware.
Users on a shared computer or network each see their own desktop, documents and preferences, and cannot see other people's private files.
The OS can set **password rules** (minimum length, change regularly) and lock accounts after repeated failed log-ins to defend against brute-force attacks.
On a network, a network manager uses user management to give a student access to the school's shared drive but not to staff files.
Why it matters: it protects confidentiality and integrity of data, and supports the Data Protection Act principle of keeping data secure (see 1.4 and 1.6).
Link to security (1.4.2): **user access levels** and **passwords** are listed as methods of preventing vulnerabilities.
core.h: User management: accounts, passwords and access rights
core.p: **User management** is the OS function that deals with the people who use the computer. It lets several users share one machine, each with a separate **account** that contains their own files and settings, and it controls what each person is allowed to do. A user proves their identity by **logging in**, normally with a username and password. The OS then applies **access rights** (permissions): an **administrator** can install software and change system settings, whereas a **standard user** can use applications and manage their own files only.

bullets: The OS lets you **create, open, save, rename, copy, move, delete and search** for files and folders.
Folders can contain other folders, forming a **hierarchical structure** (a tree). The **path** shows the route to a file, for example C:/Documents/Maths/homework.docx.
The OS records each file's **name, type (extension), size, date created/modified and location** in a directory structure so it can find the file again.
The **file extension** (e.g. .docx, .jpg, .mp3) tells the OS which application should open the file.
File management works with user management: **access rights** such as read-only or read/write stop unauthorised changes.
Over time files can be stored in scattered pieces on a hard disk; the OS can work with utility software such as defragmentation to improve this (see 1.5.2).
Good file management habits: meaningful names, a logical folder structure, regular backups.
Why it matters: without a file system the storage device would be a mass of unlabelled data with no way to find a particular file.
core.h: File management: organising and finding data
core.p: **File management** is the OS function that organises data on storage devices so that it can be found and used later. The OS provides a **file system** in which data is stored in **files** with names, grouped into **folders** (directories) arranged in a hierarchy. It keeps track of where on the disk each file is physically stored, so when you double-click a file the OS locates it, loads it into RAM and opens it in the correct program. It also provides the tools to create, name, move, copy, rename, delete and search for files, and to control who can access them.

bullets: Opening the word processor: the **file manager** finds the program, **memory management** loads it into RAM, the **UI** draws its window.
Playing music at the same time: **multitasking** gives both programs time slices of the CPU.
Saving the essay: the **file manager** writes the data to secondary storage with a name, type and location.
Printing: the application sends data to the OS, which uses the **printer driver** and a **print queue**.
Logging off: **user management** saves the settings and locks the account; memory used by the programs is **freed**.
If the printer has no driver: the OS cannot translate the print request, so printing fails; this shows how functions depend on each other.
Higher-level link: the OS also handles **security** such as stopping unauthorised access, which supports the methods in 1.4.2.
core.h: How the five functions work together: a worked scenario
core.p: Real events involve several OS functions at once, and exam scenario questions reward you for linking them. Suppose a student types an essay in a word processor, listens to music and prints the finished essay. The user interface displays the windows and passes key presses to the right program. Memory management gives both the word processor and music player their own space in RAM. Multitasking shares the CPU between them in short time slices. File management saves the essay to a folder. Peripheral management uses the printer driver to send the document to the printer, and user management ensures only this student's account can open the essay.

bullets: **Desktop/laptop OS**: full GUI, supports keyboard, mouse and many peripherals, multiple user accounts, heavy multitasking.
**Mobile OS**: touchscreen interface, app stores, power management to protect battery life, and strong restrictions on what each app can access.
**Server OS**: often used with a CLI, prioritises reliability, security and handling many users or network requests at once.
**Embedded OS**: tiny, fixed function, no need for a complicated user interface or file management.
Real-time operating systems must respond within a guaranteed time, for example in a car's braking system. (Beyond the required spec, but useful context.)
Open source (Linux) versus proprietary (Windows): see 1.6 on licensing for the effect on cost and ability to modify the code.
Exam tip: when asked which OS features a device needs, link the answer to the device's purpose (e.g. a smart thermostat does not need multi-user accounts).
core.p: Not every computer has the same type of OS, and the exam can ask you to compare. A **desktop or laptop OS** such as Windows, macOS or Linux manages a large range of hardware and many multitasking programs. A **mobile OS** such as Android or iOS is designed for touchscreens and for saving battery. An **embedded system** (such as a washing machine or car engine controller) often has a very small, specialised OS or none at all because it performs one dedicated task. All of them still perform the same fundamental jobs of managing memory, peripherals, files and the user interface, but they prioritise different things.

bullets: Memory management **protects** programs from each other, but if RAM is too small, virtual memory makes the computer slow.
Multitasking **improves productivity**, but too many programs open can make each one run slowly because the CPU time is shared.
A GUI is **easy to use** but takes more resources; a CLI is **efficient** but harder to learn.
User management **improves security**, but strict access rights can inconvenience users who need to install software.
Drivers let devices work with the OS, but a **faulty or outdated driver** may cause crashes or poor performance.
Good file management makes data easy to find, but needs users to follow naming and folder conventions.

When evaluating, finish with a **justified conclusion**, for example: 'Overall, memory management is the most important function because without it programs could overwrite each other and the system would crash'.
Always tie the answer to the **scenario**, not generic statements.
core.h: Higher-level thinking: advantages, trade-offs and evaluation
core.p: The top-band questions ask you to judge or discuss, not just list. You may be given a scenario such as a school computer room, a smartphone or a shared family PC, and asked how the OS functions help or what problems could occur. The key is to give a function, say what it does, and then state the **consequence** for the user or organisation, using words such as *because*, *so that* and *this means*. Always consider both benefits and limitations.

bullets: Make a five-row table: Function | What it does | Example | Why it matters. Fill it in from memory regularly.
Use the **name-describe-consequence** pattern: *Memory management allocates RAM to each program (describe), so programs do not overwrite each other (consequence).*
Link functions to everyday actions: opening an app (memory), clicking an icon (UI), plugging in a printer (drivers), logging in (user management), saving a file (file management).
Practise short questions from past papers: 'State two functions of an operating system' [2 marks] needs just two correct names.
For longer questions, plan using the five functions as a checklist before writing.
Be careful with similar terms: **memory management** (RAM) is not the same as **file management** (storage).
Revisit this topic with 1.4 (security) and 1.5.2 (utility software), as they are often examined together on Paper 1.
core.h: Remembering the content: structure, mnemonics and exam routine
core.p: A reliable way to remember the functions is to use a mnemonic and a standard way of answering. For example, the order **U-M-P-U-F** can stand for User interface, Memory management (and multitasking), Peripherals, User management, Files. Another approach is to attach one real-world example to each function so that you can give a concrete answer. In an exam, write the name of the function in bold, then a sentence on what it does, then a sentence on why it matters to the user. This three-part pattern earns marks on 2-, 4- and 6-mark questions.

exam: **State** (1 mark each): give a brief fact, e.g. 'State two functions of an operating system' needs two named functions such as user interface and file management.
**Describe** (2 marks): say what the function does and add one detail, e.g. 'Memory management allocates RAM to programs and stops them overwriting each other.'
**Explain** (2-3 marks): include 'because' or 'so that': 'Drivers are needed because each device understands different commands, so the OS cannot talk to it directly.'
**Discuss** (6 marks): write at least 4 functions, describe each, give a consequence, and finish with a balanced conclusion linked to the scenario.
Use the **exact terms**: 'time slices', 'allocate RAM', 'device driver', 'access rights', 'hierarchical folder structure'.
Never write 'it controls the computer' alone; this is too vague to earn a mark. Say what is controlled and how.
For GUI v CLI comparisons give a point for each side and a reason (e.g. GUI is easier but uses more memory).
Mark schemes accept different valid examples, so be specific: 'A printer driver converts the document into commands for that printer.'
In scenario questions, quote something from the scenario (e.g. 'the school has 500 students') and link the function to it.
Check the number of marks: 1 mark = one correct point; do not write a paragraph for 1 mark and do not write one line for 6 marks.
Be ready for a matching or table question: functions on one side, descriptions on the other. Learn the core description of each by heart.

mistakes.r: The OS is system software; Word is application software that runs on top of the OS.
mistakes.w: The OS is an application such as Microsoft Word.

mistakes.r: Memory management controls how RAM is allocated to programs; the hard drive is managed by file management.
mistakes.w: Memory management means looking after the hard drive.

mistakes.r: The CPU shares its time between programs in very short time slices, so they appear to run at once.
mistakes.w: Multitasking means the CPU does many things at exactly the same moment.

mistakes.r: A driver is software that lets the OS communicate with a hardware device.
mistakes.w: A driver is hardware that you plug in.

mistakes.r: The user interface is the software that lets the user interact with the computer (GUI or CLI); the monitor is an output device.
mistakes.w: The user interface is the screen or monitor.

mistakes.r: User management controls accounts, passwords and access rights; anti-malware stops viruses.
mistakes.w: User management is about stopping viruses.

mistakes.r: File management also organises, names, moves, copies, deletes, finds and secures files in a folder structure.
The OS manages resources efficiently, but its purpose is to manage the hardware and provide an interface, not to increase speed.
mistakes.w: The OS makes the computer faster.

mistakes.r: Virtual memory uses secondary storage which is slower, so heavy use slows the computer.
mistakes.w: Virtual memory is faster than RAM.

summary: OCR J277 1.5.1 asks you to explain the purpose of an operating system and describe its main functions: the user interface, memory management and multitasking, peripheral management and device drivers, user management and file management. It matters because Paper 1 regularly asks you to state, describe and discuss these functions in a scenario.

terms.d: System software that manages the computer's hardware and software resources and provides an interface for users and applications.
Software that runs and maintains the computer itself, including the operating system and utility software.
Software that allows the user to perform a task, such as a word processor or web browser.
The means by which the user interacts with the computer, for example a GUI or command line.
Graphical user interface: uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer so users can click rather than type commands.
Command-line interface: the user types text commands at a prompt.
The OS function that allocates RAM to programs, keeps their memory separate and frees it when no longer needed.
The appearance of running several programs at the same time by sharing CPU time between them in short time slices.
Part of secondary storage used as extra RAM when physical RAM is full.
A hardware device connected to the computer, such as a keyboard, mouse, monitor or printer.
Software that allows the OS to communicate with a hardware device by translating instructions between them.
The OS function that creates and controls user accounts, log-ins and access rights.
Permissions that decide what a user can open, change or delete.
The OS function that creates, organises, names, moves, copies and deletes files and folders and keeps track of where they are stored.
A container used to group files and other folders in a hierarchical structure.
The part of the OS that decides which process gets the CPU next and for how long.
A device that works automatically when connected because the OS already has a suitable driver.

worked.ans: Memory management: allocates RAM to each running program and stops programs overwriting each other's memory. User management: creates accounts and uses passwords and access rights to control what each user can do. [4 marks]
worked.q: State two functions of an operating system and describe what each does. [4 marks]
steps: Choose two functions from the specification list, e.g. memory management and user management.
Describe it: it allocates RAM to programs and keeps each program's memory separate (1 mark).
Describe it: it controls user accounts and access rights so users can only see or change what they are allowed to (1 mark).

worked.ans: The OS uses multitasking to share CPU time between the word processor and music player in short time slices, so both appear to run at once. Memory management gives each program its own area of RAM. Peripheral management uses the printer driver to translate the print request into commands for the printer. [4 marks]
worked.q: A student prints a document from a word processor while also listening to music. Explain how the operating system makes this possible. [4 marks]
steps: Identify multitasking: the CPU gives each program a short time slice and switches between them quickly (mark 1 and 2).
Identify memory management: both programs are held in separate parts of RAM so they do not interfere (mark 3).
Identify peripheral management: a printer driver translates the print request into commands the printer understands (mark 4).

worked.ans: User management gives each student their own account and password, so their work stays private, and access rights stop them installing software or changing settings, which protects the school network. File management organises each student's work in named folders in a hierarchy so files can be found, copied or deleted easily, and read-only rights can protect shared teaching resources. Together these improve security and organisation, so the system is easier to manage. [6 marks]
worked.q: A school installs new computers for students. Discuss how the operating system's user management and file management functions would be useful. [6 marks]
steps: User management: each student has a separate account and password, so work is private.
Access rights: students have standard rights so they cannot install software or change system settings; teachers/administrators have higher rights.
Consequence: this improves security and stops accidental or deliberate damage.
File management: each student's files are stored in their own folders in a hierarchical structure so they can be found quickly.
Access rights again: a shared folder can be read-only for students so they cannot delete resources.
Conclusion: together they keep data organised, secure and available only to the right people.
